scenes.title: Transit Gateway Connect: GRE, BGP and SD-WAN Integration
scenes.visual_overview: On the approved slide, titled Transit Gateway Connect: GRE, BGP and SD-WAN Integration, the numbered panels depict connect attachment placement: a supported transport attachment such as vpc or direct connect along with the architecture decisions and failure considerations.
visual_walkthrough: Connect attachment placement: a supported transport attachment such as VPC or Direct Connect
Connect peers exchange traffic over GRE and routes over BGP
GRE does not provide encryption; protect the underlying path where required
Design multiple peers, appliance resilience and both-direction routing

scenes.narration: This slide introduces Transit Gateway Connect for integrating SD-WAN or routing appliances into an AWS transit network. First, look at the top-left diagram. The Connect attachment uses an underlying supported transport attachment, such as a VPC attachment or Direct Connect attachment, rather than appearing from nowhere. Then follow the top-right diagram. Connect peers use GRE to encapsulate traffic between the Transit Gateway and the appliance, while BGP exchanges the IP routes needed for forwarding. That distinction matters: GRE carries packets, and BGP controls reachability. The bottom-left shield explicitly warns that GRE is not encryption. If the workload requires confidentiality, choose a supported protective transport or encryption layer instead of assuming the tunnel is secure by itself. Finally, the bottom-right diagram shows multiple peers and appliances. They improve resilience only with correctly engineered route advertisements, healthy appliances and return traffic. In troubleshooting, check the transport attachment, GRE endpoint addresses, BGP status, route tables, security and the reverse direction before declaring the hybrid path healthy.

scenes.title: Hybrid Operations: Prove the Complete Network Path
scenes.visual_overview: On the approved slide, titled Hybrid Operations: Prove the Complete Network Path, the numbered panels depict verify physical circuit, virtual interface, bgp state and advertised prefixes along with the architecture decisions and failure considerations.
visual_walkthrough: Verify physical circuit, virtual interface, BGP state and advertised prefixes
Inspect VPN tunnel metrics, logs, route tables, flow logs and customer router counters
Diagnose MTU or MSS when small packets succeed but large payloads stall
Test representative applications and record failover convergence, packet loss and recovery
scenes.visual_example: A hybrid AWS application follows the diagram's choices and validates both its normal workload and relevant degraded or failure condition.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The depicted architecture is usable only after its dependencies, security, routing and recovery are verified.
scenes.narration: The central stack shows that hybrid networking succeeds only when all layers work together. Begin with the first blue panel at the top left: confirm physical Direct Connect link state, virtual interface state, BGP adjacency and actual prefix visibility. An up port is not the same as a working application path. Next move to the purple panel on the upper right. For a VPN design, inspect both tunnel metrics and logs, the correct route tables, VPC Flow Logs and customer device counters. This helps separate tunnel negotiation from application forwarding. The lower-left panel illustrates a subtle symptom: pings and small packets work, but large requests or transfers stall. That can indicate path MTU discovery, encapsulation overhead or incorrect TCP MSS handling. Do not immediately rewrite a firewall policy. Finally, the lower-right panel asks for testing with realistic workloads during failure. Deliberately remove a link or tunnel, measure route convergence, packet loss and application reconnect time, and compare the result with the recovery requirement. The lesson is to prove the complete forward and return path, not merely a healthy tunnel indicator.
